extracted.intended_audience: educated early-18th-century readers of The Spectator; general readers interested in poetry and literary criticism (esp. Milton)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative guidance for reading and judging epic poetry (chiefly Milton's Paradise Lost): includes criteria on character-voice, foreshadowing, use of classical/scriptural parallels, unity of action, moral exemplars, and poetic diction. Aimed at assessing poetic art and moral fitness of scenes and speeches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artful preparation / foreshadowing
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should prepare the reader for several occurrences by founding later events upon earlier circumstances, foreshadowing without anticipating the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison praises Milton for founding the first part of Book V upon previously mentioned circumstance (the evil spirit practising upon Eve) and for presaging the catastrophe of the poem "so artfully shadow'd, that they do not anticipate the Story which follows in the ninth Book." Foreshadowing must hint at outcomes while preserving surprise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-voice must suit moral/state of person
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches and sentiments assigned to characters must be appropriate to their moral condition and station; avoid incongruous flattery or falsehood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: "An injudicious Poet would have made Adam talk thro the whole Work in such Sentiments as these: But Flattery and Falshood are not the Courtship of Milton's Adam..." — Addison argues Adam's manner should not be full of courtly flattery in his state of innocence. Later: Raphael converses "as one Friend converses with another," matching his dignity and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action in the epic
rubrics_metrics.description: The epic must preserve unity of action regardless of how one dates the action's beginning (immediate or remote).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison insists the unity of Milton's action is preserved whether you take the revolt in Heaven or the infernal council as the beginning; unity should be maintained even when episodes exist (e.g., the sacking of Troy regarded as an episode in the Æneid).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of classical and scriptural parallels (judicious imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet may echo or imitate passages from Scripture or classical poets (Homer, Canticles, Ezekiel) but should do so with judgment and aptness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison notes Milton frequently has his eye on the Song of Solomon and Homer, and defends marvellous machinery (gates that open, living wheels) by parallel passages in Scripture (Ezekiel). Imitation must justify the marvellous and be employed with "usual Judgment."

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity to authoritative sources balanced with invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions (especially of supernatural or sacred subjects) should be conformable to Scripture or traditional authority while still allowing strong imaginative invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Milton's angels are praised as "so finely drawn, and so conformable to the Notions which are given of them in Scripture," yet he adds original touches (e.g., the image "Like Maia's Son he stood, / And shook his Plumes, that Heavnly Fragrance fill'd"). Both fidelity and novelty are virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force of imagination and variety of circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative and descriptive passages should display great force of imagination and a fine variety of circumstances to sustain interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to the Revolt in Heaven: Addison commends Milton's powerful imagination and variety, and his successful imitation of Homeric grandeur where appropriate (e.g., the image of Satan's palace).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elevation of ordinary/domestic subjects by poetic language
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should be able to set off mundane or domestic activities with pleasing images and strong expression, making them agreeable and poetically worthy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison praises Milton's description of Eve's housewifry: though the subject is household tasks, it is "set off with so many pleasing Images and strong Expressions, as make it none of the least agreeable Parts in this Divine Work."

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and effect of devotional/hymnic passages
rubrics_metrics.description: Devotional hymns or invocations within an epic should suit the context and awaken a proper religious enthusiasm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Morning Hymn is lauded as proper for first parents: invoking parts of creation is apt worship and "awaken[s] that Divine Enthusiasm" — devotional passages should fill the mind with glorious ideas of God's works and be fitting to the characters' circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral exemplars as instructive characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters who preserve virtue amid corruption should be drawn as noble exemplars, providing a moral lesson to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison singles out Abdiel for his 'noble Moral of religious Singularity' — his steadfast loyalty among the faithless is presented as a pattern for readers living in degeneracy and corruption. Poetic characters can serve didactic ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding overwrought or inconsistent dream-logic when not intended
rubrics_metrics.description: Dream-sequences should display the wildness and inconsistency natural to dreams, but should not undermine overall coherence or seem gratuitously extravagant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On Eve's dream, Addison says the vision is "founded upon Truth" yet its circumstances are "full of that Wildness and Inconsistency which are natural to a Dream." The poet may use dream-logic but must keep it purposeful and artful.
